meaning: The AWS service that runs the Slurm controller for you and launches EC2 instances in your account for the jobs you submit.
A job scheduler widely used in high-performance computing. It holds the waiting jobs and decides which job runs on which machines.
The field that runs simulations and model training across many machines at once.
The Slurm process that holds the list of waiting jobs and allocates nodes to them. In PCS, AWS runs it in one of three sizes.
A machine that runs jobs. In PCS, each compute node is one EC2 instance that runs slurmd and the PCS agent.
The Slurm daemon that runs on each compute node and takes orders from the controller.
A named Slurm queue in front of a set of nodes. Each PCS queue is one partition.
The PCS object that users submit jobs to. It is one Slurm partition, and it points at one or more compute node groups.
The PCS object that describes how nodes are created: the instance types, the minimum and maximum instance count, the subnets, the image and one purchase option.
The Slurm command that submits a shell script as a job and returns at once.
The Slurm command that starts a program on every node that a job was given.
The Slurm command that lists jobs and shows the state of each one.
The Slurm command that queries the accounting record of past jobs.
One Slurm submission that expands into many numbered copies of the same script. Slurm schedules each copy as its own job.
How Slurm counts resources that are neither CPU cores nor memory. GPUs are the main example.
The job states that squeue shows: PD while the job waits, CF while its nodes are being brought up, and R while it runs.
An optional PCS log that records each node as LAUNCHED, REGISTERED, ACTIVE or TERMINATED, together with a reason.
The PCS setting for how long a node may sit idle before PCS removes it. The default is 600 seconds.
Putting a job that lost its node back in the queue. The job then starts again from the first line of its script.
A feature is a label on a group's nodes, and a constraint is the job option that asks for nodes with that label. A job uses them to choose a group when several groups serve one queue.
The always-on machine where users type Slurm commands. In PCS, it is a static compute node group that is attached to no queue.
An EC2 object that holds the instance settings a compute node group cannot express itself, such as EFA interfaces, the placement group, capacity reservations and user data.
The script that an EC2 instance runs when it boots. In this section, it mounts the shared file system.
The disk image that an EC2 instance boots from.
The EC2 network device that lets processes on different nodes exchange data without passing through the operating system's network stack.
The EC2 placement setting that AWS recommends for a compute node group that uses EFA.
A managed parallel file system built for many nodes that read and write large files at the same time.
A managed NFS share. In this section, it holds the home directories.
Your private network in AWS. The cluster's nodes run inside it.
The unit EC2 uses to size an instance's processor.
A reservation that holds EC2 instances of one type for you, so that the capacity is there when a group launches.
A block of GPU instances booked in advance for a fixed period.
A P6e-GB200 or P6e-GB300 machine that joins many GPUs with NVLink.
NVIDIA's direct connection between GPUs.
The NVIDIA service that lets GPUs in different nodes share memory. On PCS, each job needs an IMEX domain of its own.
A script that PCS runs on a node at one of two boot stages: nodeBootstrapped, before slurmd starts, or nodeReady, after it starts.
AWS's other way to build a Slurm cluster. Its boot hooks map onto PCS node lifecycle actions.
A model that learns to predict what the robot's cameras will show next. In this section, training it is the multi-node job of the worked example.
